chapter_theme: The first half of the heading இல்வாழ்க்கை, eleven verses on the household: money as the seed of its work, cherishing the wife who shared its toil, keeping up appearances in want, the wife who tends guests unbidden, the father's charge over his children, a mother's favour, the bard who pleads for a straying husband, a glance that hides modesty, not entering a friend's house alone, the futility of confining women, and the great sparing the poor as hosts.

327.reading: The verse says, to a woman, that womanhood of great charm is not without modesty, the life of the body is not without food, and the household's undertakings cannot be carried out without money, and clinches it with the proverb that there is no conjuring trick without a seed.
327.nuance: The first two clauses are given as plain preconditions so that the third, money for the work of the house, takes their certainty. சம்பிரதம் is a juggler's or conjuror's feat, most likely the trick of making a plant spring up, which still needs a real seed: even the marvel has a material cause. The line on modesty is a statement of the period about what makes a woman, not a counsel the reading endorses.

norm.note: a norm of the period that a woman's womanhood requires modesty

pazhamozhi.literal: there is no conjuring feat without a seed

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to any undertaking that seems to come from nothing

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the work of the household needs money as its seed

328.reading: The verse says that wives who have shared the toil of the household with their husbands are, once this is seen, to be cherished without parting, and that men who are not content with what they themselves have obtained and keep reaching for more are like those who dig too deep and come upon a snake.
328.nuance: உரிமை is the wife's right place in the house, and உழந்தமை is labour shared there, so her claim to be kept is earned by toil. Who 'does not rejoice in what they got' is not stated; read with the proverb it is most likely the husband who looks past the wife he has, and over-digging finds harm, but it could be read of anyone discontented with his lot.

pazhamozhi.literal: if one digs too deep, there are some who see a snake

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the man who seeks beyond what he has

pazhamozhi.applied_to: discontent with one's own lot and partner turns up harm

329.reading: The verse says that even when the ruin within the house is great one should keep a bright face outside, and even when one has no bed at all, since nobody asks those who are well dressed whether they have eaten.
329.nuance: The proverb is an observation about how the world reads people, not a moral claim: the clothed are presumed fed. The counsel is the household's dignity before others, and it accepts concealment of want as part of it.

pazhamozhi.literal: no one asks those who are clothed about their food

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the impoverished house that keeps up its outer show

pazhamozhi.applied_to: keeping one's outward state hides an inner want

330.reading: The verse says that those whose wife, by nature reading the unspoken sign, tends the guests who come and who live secure in their wealth without trouble have, as it were, set up a water-lift in the sea every day.
330.nuance: The wife acts on what the husband has not said (சொல்லாமை நோக்கிக் குறிப்பறியும்), so the hospitality is hers. துலாம் here is the counterpoised pole that lifts water from a well; set up in the sea it never runs dry. Line 2 reads விரும்தோம்பி, a slip for விருந்தோம்பி.

pazhamozhi.literal: they have set up a water-lift in the sea

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the house whose wife tends guests

pazhamozhi.applied_to: such a house draws from a store that does not fail

331.reading: The verse says, to a deer-eyed woman, that by whatever means the head of the house must make his children stand on the right path, for the doll one has made oneself becomes a thing that afflicts its maker.
331.nuance: இறைவன் here is the master of the house, the father, not a god or a king. அணங்கு can be a goddess or an afflicting spirit; with the warning of the first lines it is most likely the latter, so the child one formed carelessly becomes one's own torment, but the proverb could also say that what one shapes well becomes one's object of worship.

pazhamozhi.literal: the doll one made becomes an afflicting spirit to oneself

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the parent and the child he forms

pazhamozhi.applied_to: a father answers for the children he shapes

332.reading: The verse says that at dice, though the wealth staked on both sides is equal, an onlooker at the side leans to one player, and that so even among children who are all of great worth a mother has one she favours, asking whether mothers' sides among their children are any different.
332.nuance: The proverb is a question; read with the dice image it grants that partiality is natural even where merit is equal, rather than condemning it. The first line's ஒக்கும் வகையான் உடன்பொருள் is compressed and the grammar of line 2 is loose, so the dice scene is reconstructed.

pazhamozhi.literal: is a mother's leaning among her children anything other?

story.act: the bystander at a game of dice who takes one player's side though the stakes are equal

pazhamozhi.applied_to: favour among equals is natural, even to a mother

333.reading: The verse has a wife tell the bard that while her husband presses his body to the breasts of bangled young women he should not speak what is not the way, since no one can wake a man who only feigns sleep.
333.nuance: This is an akam situation set under the household heading: the bard comes to plead for the husband who keeps courtesans. The proverb of feigned sleep is most likely said of the husband, who strays knowingly and cannot be reformed by words, though it may also be her refusal to be taken in by the bard's excuses.
333.domain_note: a wife answering the bard who pleads for her husband

pazhamozhi.literal: one who feigns sleep is hard for anyone to wake

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the husband who goes to courtesans knowing what he does

pazhamozhi.applied_to: a man who strays by choice will not be turned by pleading

334.reading: The verse says that the startled-doe gaze of finely jewelled women hides the modesty that lives in it, as a garland spoils another garland, and closes that this is how excellence cuts excellence.
334.nuance: The sense is that one beauty, the frightened glance, covers another, the modesty, so that a grace is lost to sight by a grace; but line 3 (தொழுதையுள் மாலையும் மாலை மறுக்குறுத்தாள்) is obscure, and both who 'spoiled the garland' and what the garland stands for are guesses. The counsel has little to do with the household heading.

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to a woman's glance that hides her modesty

335.reading: The verse says that even men of pure mind should not enter alone even the house of a friend, because when the town is loud with talk of wrong no witness can stand, as no dam holds when the water rises.
335.nuance: The innocence of the man is granted: the point is that the town's clamour is a flood, and a pure mind is no defence against it. கரி is a witness; the line says that once rumour rises there is none who can testify to the truth.

pazhamozhi.literal: when the water rises there is no dam

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to rumour overwhelming the innocent

pazhamozhi.applied_to: avoid the occasion, for a rumour once loosed cannot be checked

336.reading: The verse says that women of fine jewels who excel by their own restraint cannot be held by confinement, and that one without it, though bound by force until she suffers, is like a dog's tail, which never comes straight.
336.nuance: Lines 1 and 2 and the proverb face two ways: the woman with நிறை needs no prison, and the one without is not changed by it. The verse keeps the assumption that women's conduct is a matter for guarding and says only that force cannot do it.
336.domain_note: the husband who would guard a wife

norm.note: a norm of the period on guarding women's chastity by confinement

pazhamozhi.literal: a dog's tail never becomes straight

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the woman without restraint whom force cannot amend

pazhamozhi.applied_to: confinement neither makes nor mends a woman's restraint

337.reading: The verse says that those who have grown very great should not go as passing guests to the poor, for the strain of those who give beyond their means is like a sparrow cutting its own thigh, whose entrails faint.
337.nuance: The duty is laid on the guest, not the host: the poor man will feed a great guest beyond his means, so the great should spare him. குறங்கு is the thigh; the sparrow that cuts its own flesh to feed others (perhaps its young) has so little that it collapses.
337.domain_note: the great who visit the poor

pazhamozhi.literal: when the sparrow cuts its thigh, its entrails faint

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the poor host who gives more than he has

pazhamozhi.applied_to: a great guest ruins the poor host who must receive him

links.note: Kural 247 grants as plain fact that this world is not for those without wealth; Pazhamozhi 327 brings that fact into the house and sets money beside a woman's modesty and the body's food as a precondition of the household's work.
links.teaches: Read together, the couplet's premise about wealth and this world becomes a rule of the house: money is one of three things a household life cannot do without.
links.list_adds: its run of three 'not without' clauses ranks money with modesty and food, so wealth stands as one of the household's basic needs rather than a worldly power.

links.note: Kural 85 asks whether the field of one who feeds guests even needs sowing; Pazhamozhi 330 gives the same unfailing yield to the house, but credits the hospitality to the wife who reads the husband's unspoken sign.
links.teaches: The pair shows the promise of endless plenty for the hospitable house resting in practice on the wife, whose silent understanding of her husband is what keeps the guests fed.
links.list_adds: its proverb of a water-lift in the sea replaces the unsown field with an inexhaustible source, and it adds the wife's reading of signs, which the couplet does not mention.

links.note: Kural 67 names the father's good to his son as setting him first in the assembly; Pazhamozhi 331 makes the father's task the child's conduct and warns that a child badly formed afflicts the one who formed him.
links.teaches: Together they give the father's duty a reward and a penalty: the well-formed son is set before the assembly, the ill-formed one turns on the father like a made thing become a demon.
links.list_adds: its proverb of the doll that becomes an afflicting spirit to its maker adds the cost of failure, which the couplet's statement of the duty leaves unsaid.

links.note: Kural 57 says confinement is no use and a woman's own நிறை is the best guard; Pazhamozhi 336 restates this and adds the obverse, that a woman without that restraint is not amended by force however hard.
links.teaches: The couplet shows only that the inner guard is better; the verse makes the outer guard useless in both cases, needless for the restrained and powerless over the unrestrained.
links.list_adds: its dog's-tail proverb supplies the second case the couplet does not state, so the claim covers both the woman with restraint and the woman without it.

links.note: Nanmanikkadigai 90 says a woman without a bond goes as she pleases though guarded; Pazhamozhi 336 says the same of confinement and closes it with the dog's tail.
links.teaches: The counted verse sets the woman beside desire and hidden murder as natures that outrun control; the proverb makes the same point by a household image of a crookedness force cannot straighten.

links.note: In Akananuru 146 the wife refuses the bard sent to plead for the husband who goes to the courtesans' street; Pazhamozhi 333 sets the same refusal of the bard in four lines and closes it with the proverb that a feigned sleeper cannot be woken.
links.teaches: The ethics work takes the akam wife's refusal of the bard and turns it into a general judgement, that a husband who strays knowingly is beyond persuasion, where the Sangam poem left the charge in images and pity.

links.note: Kural 693 tells the king's servant that once suspicion has arisen nobody can clear it; Pazhamozhi 335 carries the same irreversibility into a friend's house, where the town's rumour leaves no witness.
links.teaches: The pairing shows one rule about suspicion working at court and in the town alike: since it cannot be undone, the only defence is avoiding the occasion, even for the innocent.
links.list_adds: its flood-and-dam proverb gives the couplet's 'hard for anyone' a cause, the swell of public talk, and moves it from the king's suspicion to the neighbours'.

links.note: Naladiyar 141 says the well-born keep their principles though their clothes are rags; Pazhamozhi 329 says the household should keep a bright outward show even in ruin, since the world reads want from dress.
links.teaches: The two divide dignity in poverty between inner principle, which must never fall, and outward appearance, which the Naladiyar lets go and the Pazhamozhi insists on keeping for the world's eyes.
links.list_adds: its proverb about the clothed never being asked if they have eaten adds the social reason for outward show, which the quatrain's lion image of inner nature ignores.

links.note: Kural 90 warns the host that a guest wilts at a changed face; Pazhamozhi 337 turns the duty on the guest: the great should not stay with the poor, whom hospitality strains beyond their means.
links.teaches: Read together, hospitality has two delicate parties: the guest who wilts at a cold look and the poor host who would wound himself to feed a great guest.
links.list_adds: its sparrow proverb names the host's cost, which the Kural's chapter on hospitality never counts, and makes restraint a guest's virtue.

source_issues: 330 line 2: விரும்தோம்பி is a misspelling of விருந்தோம்பி.
334 line 3: தொழுதையுள் மாலையும் மாலை மறுக்குறுத்தாள் is obscure and may be corrupt; the verse's sense is uncertain.
332 lines 1-2: the dice comparison is compressed and its grammar loose.
